Westward
wĕst'wărd
adv. and a. (toward the west; in the tabernacle, the closed end — the side where the holy of holies stood and no door was)
From west (Anglo-Saxon west, the quarter of the sunset) plus -ward. Hebrew has no separate word for the west: it says yam, the sea, because the Mediterranean lay westward of the land, and it says achor, behind, because a man facing east has the west at his back.

Biblical Definition

Westward in the Law is nearly always structural, and its structure preaches. The tabernacle's west end is closed: “for the sides of the tabernacle westward thou shalt make six boards” (Exo 26:22) — boards, not a curtain and not a door. The most holy place stood at that end, and there was no way in from behind. Only one man, once a year, with blood, entered from the east through the veil. Behind that closed wall camped the Gershonites: “The families of the Gershonites shall pitch behind the tabernacle westward” (Num 3:23). The word also marks the boundary of sight and of longing. Abram is told to look “northward, and southward, and eastward, and westward” (Gen 13:14) and given all he sees; Moses on Pisgah is told to lift his eyes “westward, and northward, and southward, and eastward, and behold it with thine eyes: for thou shalt not go over this Jordan” (Deu 3:27) — the same four directions, the same gift of sight, and a man who will see the land and not enter it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines westward as toward the west, and the west as the quarter where the sun sets, the point directly opposite to the east.

expand to see more

WESTWARD, adv. Toward the west; as, to sail westward.

WEST, n. That point of the horizon where the sun sets at the equinox; or the corresponding point of the earth.

2. A region or country lying in that direction.

Note. In the Hebrew the west is denoted by the sea, the Mediterranean lying west of Judea, and also by the word signifying behind.

Key Scripture

Exo 26:22 — "And for the sides of the tabernacle westward thou shalt make six boards."

Num 3:23 — "The families of the Gershonites shall pitch behind the tabernacle westward."

Deu 3:27 — "Get thee up into the top of Pisgah, and lift up thine eyes westward, and northward, and southward, and eastward, and behold it with thine eyes: for thou shalt not go over this Jordan."

Gen 13:14 — "And the LORD said unto Abram, after that Lot was separated from him, Lift up now thine eyes, and look from the place where thou art northward, and southward, and eastward, and westward:"

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that God appointed one way into His presence and closed every other.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. No movement disputes which way is west. What has been lost is the doctrine the tabernacle's closed west end was built to teach: that access to God is not available on every side, that the sinner does not select his own approach, and that the one way in is the way God appointed. Exo 26:22 specifies boards where a man might have expected an opening, and the specification is deliberate. Behind the mercy seat there was a wall.

The principle to recover is exclusivity of access, which the New Testament does not abolish but fulfils. “I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (Joh 14:6); “having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way” (Heb 10:19-20). The veil is torn and the way is open — but it is still a way, singular, and it is still the one God opened. Deu 3:27 supplies the sober companion truth: Moses saw the whole land from Pisgah, in every direction, and did not enter. Sight is not possession, and no amount of looking substitutes for the appointed entrance.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

English west + -ward; rendering Hebrew yam (H3220), the sea, used for the west quarter, and achor (H268), the hinder part.

expand to see more

Hebrew yam (H3220) — sea; used for “west” because the Great Sea lay west of the land. “Westward” in Exo 26:22 is literally “seaward”.

Hebrew achor (H268) — the hinder part, behind; the west is behind a man facing the sunrise.

Hebrew maarab (H4628) — the setting, the west; from arab, to grow dark, whence also evening.

Psa 103:12 — “as far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us”; the one pair of directions with no meeting point.

Num 3:23-38 — the four Levite camps by compass: Gershon west, Kohath south, Merari north, Moses and Aaron east at the door.

Usage

"“For the sides of the tabernacle westward… six boards” — a wall where a man might expect a door."

"“Pitch behind the tabernacle westward” — the Gershonites at the closed end."

"“Lift up thine eyes westward… for thou shalt not go over” — sight granted, entrance withheld."
